item.title: United Airlines CEO: 'We should have a national wealth tax'
item.author: Molly Moorhead
item.description:
United Airlines CEO: 'We should have a national wealth tax'
2026-10-21
Por Molly Moorhead
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/united-airlines-ceo-we-should-have-a-national-wealth-tax-092341353.html
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby gave a wide-ranging, often provocative interview to the New York Times, defending fees for aisle and window seats and countering the rise in airfares by asserting "it's expensive to fly airplanes."
"There are customers that pay more that get more," Kirby, 59, said in the interview that ran Oct. 18.
But he struck a decidedly more populist note on the topic of wealth inequality — which he brought up when the Times asked him about waning trust in CEOs and his responsibility in dispelling it. Here's his full answer:
"Wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that," he said. "We should have a national wealth tax — it won't work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them."
United Airlines stock rose 0.3% before the bell on Tuesday.
Kirby is not the first or only business titan to call for bigger taxes on the wealthiest Americans. Luminaries like Warren Buffett, Bill Gates, and George Soros have long advocated for increasing the tax burden at their rarefied wealth levels.
Read more: How much does a millionaire actually owe the IRS on tax day?
"We've updated our tax system before to keep up with changing times, and we need to do it again, starting with raising taxes on people like me," Gates wrote on his blog in 2020.
Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce (CRM), wrote in 2019 that "increasing taxes on high-income individuals like myself would help generate the trillions of dollars that we desperately need to improve education and healthcare and fight climate change."
Joe Biden was president, and Democrats in Congress were gearing up to pass legislation to tax unrealized gains on individuals with a net worth of at least $1 billion or annual income of $100 million for three consecutive years. Of course, that never happened, and after President Trump was reelected, Republicans in Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included provisions that made lower marginal tax rates for high incomes permanent, along with other provisions benefiting wealthy Americans.
Read more: 10 ways the One Big Beautiful Bill Act affects student loans and financial aid
As for the inheritance taxes Kirby said he favors, there is no federal tax on individual beneficiaries of inherited assets. A few states impose a state inheritance tax.
There is a federal estate tax, but the exemption is so large — $15 million per person — that few people ever pay it. Only 0.2% of estates are large enough to be subject to the tax, and even then the tax applies only to the amount that exceeds the exemption threshold.
Molly Moorhead is economics editor for Yahoo Finance.

item.content:encoded:
United Airlines CEO: 'We should have a national wealth tax'

2026-10-21

Por Molly Moorhead

https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/united-airlines-ceo-we-should-have-a-national-wealth-tax-092341353.html

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby gave a wide-ranging, often provocative interview to the New York Times, defending fees for aisle and window seats and countering the rise in airfares by asserting "it's expensive to fly airplanes."

"There are customers that pay more that get more," Kirby, 59, said in the interview that ran Oct. 18.

But he struck a decidedly more populist note on the topic of wealth inequality — which he brought up when the Times asked him about waning trust in CEOs and his responsibility in dispelling it. Here's his full answer:

"Wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that," he said. "We should have a national wealth tax — it won't work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them."

United Airlines stock rose 0.3% before the bell on Tuesday.

Kirby is not the first or only business titan to call for bigger taxes on the wealthiest Americans. Luminaries like Warren Buffett, Bill Gates, and George Soros have long advocated for increasing the tax burden at their rarefied wealth levels.

Read more: How much does a millionaire actually owe the IRS on tax day?

"We've updated our tax system before to keep up with changing times, and we need to do it again, starting with raising taxes on people like me," Gates wrote on his blog in 2020.

Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce (CRM), wrote in 2019 that "increasing taxes on high-income individuals like myself would help generate the trillions of dollars that we desperately need to improve education and healthcare and fight climate change."

Joe Biden was president, and Democrats in Congress were gearing up to pass legislation to tax unrealized gains on individuals with a net worth of at least $1 billion or annual income of $100 million for three consecutive years. Of course, that never happened, and after President Trump was reelected, Republicans in Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included provisions that made lower marginal tax rates for high incomes permanent, along with other provisions benefiting wealthy Americans.

Read more: 10 ways the One Big Beautiful Bill Act affects student loans and financial aid

As for the inheritance taxes Kirby said he favors, there is no federal tax on individual beneficiaries of inherited assets. A few states impose a state inheritance tax.

There is a federal estate tax, but the exemption is so large — $15 million per person — that few people ever pay it. Only 0.2% of estates are large enough to be subject to the tax, and even then the tax applies only to the amount that exceeds the exemption threshold.

Molly Moorhead is economics editor for Yahoo Finance.

item.title: Great Scott! The AI-fueled data center build-out could double next year: Chart of the Day
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Great Scott! The AI-fueled data center build-out could double next year: Chart of the Day
2026-10-21
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/great-scott-the-ai-fueled-data-center-build-out-could-double-next-year-chart-of-the-day-100000440.html
Doc Brown needed 1.21 gigawatts to send a DeLorean through time in the 1985 movie "Back to the Future." The data-center industry could add about 42 times that next year.
Welcome to the Doc Brown Index.
Research firm SemiAnalysis expects annual additions to data center IT capacity outside China to more than double next year, to about 51 gigawatts from 25 gigawatts this year.
In movie units, that's about 21 Doc Browns ballooning to 42. These are additions in a single year, not the whole fleet or the electricity it uses. By SemiAnalysis's count, that one year would roughly match the world's entire data center build-out through 2024.
About three-quarters of next year's projected additions come from projects already operational or under construction. The rest are still planned. SemiAnalysis points to more than 24 gigawatts across 40 campuses in advanced construction for expected delivery next year.
Not everyone buys it. At the All-In Summit in September, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner called SemiAnalysis's forecast at the time, 43 gigawatts, too aggressive and guessed the industry would stand up closer to 25 gigawatts. That's only about 21 Doc Browns — no faster than this year.
How do you build that much, that quickly? Increasingly, in pieces.
Suppliers now build electrical rooms and cooling systems in factories while crews prepare the site. SemiAnalysis calls the results Lego data centers, with bricks that can weigh 50,000 pounds.
Amazon (AMZN) is rolling out its own modular design at large scale, and Meta Platforms (META) has put up tent-like halls to enclose buildings faster, according to SemiAnalysis.
A SemiAnalysis model of a 50-megawatt AI data hall puts conventional construction at 22 months and a fully modular approach at 14, excluding permitting. The biggest saving comes from electrical and mechanical installation. For the owner of the chips inside, SemiAnalysis values that eight-month head start at about $200 million.
That shift puts suppliers in the race alongside chipmakers such as Nvidia (NVDA). SemiAnalysis estimates content per megawatt for Vertiv (VRT) roughly doubles, to as much as $7 million, when it sells the full modular stack. Contractors Comfort Systems USA (FIX) and Sterling Infrastructure (STRL) assemble modules too.
But a finished building still needs power.
Microsoft (MSFT) confirmed Monday that it pulled out of a lease at a planned 50-megawatt Nscale data center outside London — the same size as the SemiAnalysis model — after grid officials said power might not arrive until the 2030s. Microsoft said the decision involved a single site and that its broader partnership with Nscale continues.

item.title: Walmart goes on offense to win the subscription space, offering new bundle for one price
item.author: Brooke DiPalma
item.description:
Walmart goes on offense to win the subscription space, offering new bundle for one price
2026-10-21
Por Brooke DiPalma
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/walmart-goes-on-offense-to-win-the-subscription-space-offering-new-bundle-for-one-price-100000929.html
As many Americans say they're strapped by subscription fatigue, Walmart is looking to make its offerings more enticing by combining Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus for $120 a year, plus tax.
The all-in-one offering announced Tuesday is only available annually, with no monthly option or trial. If you were to purchase each offer separately, Walmart+ costs $98 plus tax per year, or $12.95 plus tax per month, and its wholesale membership, Sam's Club Plus, costs $120 a year. A basic club membership runs $60.
Walmart (WMT) posted its slowest US same-store sales growth last quarter since Q4 of 2020, at 2.6%. Now the retailer is hoping it can recapture share it may have lost to others like Target (TGT), Amazon (AMZN), Costco (COST), and BJ's (BJ).
"We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships … we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a release.
Here's how Walmart's subscription bundle compares with competitors:
Target Circle 360 is $4.99 per month or $49 per year. Amazon Prime costs $140 a year.
A standard Costco membership runs $65 a year, whereas the executive membership costs $130. For a standard BJ's membership, it's $60 per year or $120 for BJ's Club+.
The membership model is a sizeable opportunity for Walmart, per Bank of America analyst Christopher Nardone, who said in a recent note, "Walmart+ members spend approximately 4x more compared to non-members."
He added that advertising, marketplace growth, and global membership remain healthy and reaffirmed confidence "that the broader flywheel to improve longer-term profitability remains intact. "
He added, "These businesses give Walmart an advantage to navigate the challenging pricing and supply chain environment in the near term, but longer-term continued execution across these businesses should help improve longer-term profitability versus today's levels."
Deutsche Bank analyst Krisztina Katai recently upgraded the stock to a Buy rating from Neutral, citing that "the current inflationary environment should reinforce Walmart's value proposition and support accelerated share gains."
All employees will now get both memberships to Walmart and Sam's Club as part of their benefits. Last week, the company announced plans to cover over 250 medications, including insulin and inhalers for $0 and GLP-1s for diabetes.
Brooke DiPalma is a reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on X at @BrookeDiPalma or email her at bdipalma@yahoofinance.com.

item.title: Meta and Google are about to have a consumer AI showdown
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
Meta and Google are about to have a consumer AI showdown
2026-10-21
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/meta-and-google-are-about-to-have-a-consumer-ai-showdown-100000834.html
The race to put out a widely adopted and highly competent digital assistant is a fight to control the next popular tech platform. It just so happens that the companies poised for a heated confrontation over AI agents are also the two dominant digital advertising firms.
Meta (META), which reports quarterly results Tuesday, and Google (GOOG) are headed for an AI showdown.
Last month Meta's Muse burst onto the scene, delivering the first popular AI agent for normies, and just cracked a download milestone. Muse's early success, in both downloads and praise, previewed a world where more people rely on their digital helpers to get work done and manage their daily routines.
More cautious tech users might wait for the first wave of early adopters to find the bugs and iron out the kinks. The trust that goes with safeguarding emails, calendars, and wallets hasn't historically been Meta's purview. Better to hold out for whatever consumer-focused agent the iPhone maker or the Gmail company has in store.
First-mover status has won Meta public goodwill and an upward jolt in its stock price. Still, that hasn't made the threat from its advertising rival any less potent.
Several analysts have said that Google's future agent offering is a key risk facing Meta. Being first is often good enough in the tech world. But what comes second can be better — or more trusted. And in the uncharted territory of new AI services, early, tech-oriented users are likely to be different from the masses of people who enter the market later on.
"Google remains well positioned to lead in the AI era supported by proprietary models, custom silicon & broad product distribution," wrote Bank of America analysts led by Justin Post in a note earlier this week. He added that a competitive agent and broader Gemini 4 launch could be catalysts for the search giant.
Another point of tension between Meta and Google is how their legacy businesses can help or hurt their AI ambitions.
Google and Meta are the top dogs in the digital advertising market. They account for more than half of global ad revenue. But one of the crucial ideas behind AI agents is moving away from a screen-phone-app interface. Mobile apps prospered because they allowed for an easier, more intuitive form of computing. AI agents, taken to the extreme, promise to do away with computing altogether, or at least in the way we are used to.

item.title: Trump announces $8 billion for farmers to offset soaring diesel costs
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Trump announces $8 billion for farmers to offset soaring diesel costs
2026-10-21
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/trump-announces-8-billion-for-farmers-to-offset-soaring-diesel-costs-111330890.html
President Trump announced an $8 billion aid package on Monday to help US farmers pay for diesel this harvest season.
The relief program, announced at a campaign rally in Kansas and on social media, aims to bring down fuel costs for Americans ahead of next month's midterm elections.
"Tonight, I am also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new 'Harvest Fuel Relief Program,' providing our Farmers with 8 BILLION DOLLARS in support to offset Diesel costs during this Harvest Season," Trump's account posted on Truth Social (DJT).
"When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our Great Farmers, and Fuel prices will come tumbling down as soon as the Iran War is over, which will happen very quickly!" he added.
The Harvest Fuel Relief Program will be administered by the US Department of Agriculture. Trump credited Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas with helping advance the initiative.
The White House move comes as nearly every corner of the economy, including farming and transportation, grapples with soaring energy input costs.
Diesel prices on Tuesday hovered near a national average of about $6.32 per gallon after hitting a record high in September, driven by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as constrained global refining capacity.
Read more: The US economy is facing 2 hot wars heating up at a bad time for the White House
The aid program won't directly lower fuel costs but will provide one-time payments through the USDA's Farm Service Agency (FSA) to help farmers offset these expenses.

item.content:encoded:
Trump announces $8 billion for farmers to offset soaring diesel costs

2026-10-21

Por Ines Ferré

https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/trump-announces-8-billion-for-farmers-to-offset-soaring-diesel-costs-111330890.html

President Trump announced an $8 billion aid package on Monday to help US farmers pay for diesel this harvest season.

The relief program, announced at a campaign rally in Kansas and on social media, aims to bring down fuel costs for Americans ahead of next month's midterm elections.

"Tonight, I am also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new 'Harvest Fuel Relief Program,' providing our Farmers with 8 BILLION DOLLARS in support to offset Diesel costs during this Harvest Season," Trump's account posted on Truth Social (DJT).

"When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our Great Farmers, and Fuel prices will come tumbling down as soon as the Iran War is over, which will happen very quickly!" he added.

The Harvest Fuel Relief Program will be administered by the US Department of Agriculture. Trump credited Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas with helping advance the initiative.

The White House move comes as nearly every corner of the economy, including farming and transportation, grapples with soaring energy input costs.

Diesel prices on Tuesday hovered near a national average of about $6.32 per gallon after hitting a record high in September, driven by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as constrained global refining capacity.

Read more: The US economy is facing 2 hot wars heating up at a bad time for the White House

The aid program won't directly lower fuel costs but will provide one-time payments through the USDA's Farm Service Agency (FSA) to help farmers offset these expenses.

Earlier this month, the Trump administration moved to lift restrictions on red-dyed diesel, a tax-exempt fuel typically reserved for tractors and farm gear. The measure allows its use in standard highway vehicles.

Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

item.title: US housing market likely to stay bleak, Goldman Sachs warns
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
US housing market likely to stay bleak, Goldman Sachs warns
2026-10-21
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/us-housing-market-likely-to-stay-bleak-goldman-sachs-warns-133222926.html
US housing market conditions are unlikely to change much just because the calendar turns from 2026 to 2027, Goldman Sachs warned.
Elevated mortgage rates will keep homeownership out of reach for many Americans and, in turn, weigh on the US economy.
"In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability — reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates — to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Goldman Sachs analyst Ronnie Walker said. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months. More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have interest rates below current market rates, and 65% have rates 2 percentage points below market rates, strongly disincentivizing them from moving."
Read more: How to get the lowest mortgage rates right now
Walker estimated existing home sales of just 3.9 million in 2027, 26% below 2019 levels and slightly shy of his 4 million estimate for 2026.
"We expect housing demand to remain tepid," Walker added.
The housing affordability crisis is likely to continue to weigh on young people looking to buy a home.
About 9 in 10 adults younger than 40 say it's harder for young adults today to buy a home than it was for their parents' generation, according to a recent Pew Research Center survey.
Since 2019, home prices in the US have risen faster than young adults' incomes, according to the Pew Research data.
Between 2019 and 2024, the inflation-adjusted median home value rose 30%, Pew noted, while the inflation-adjusted median household income for households headed by those under 40 rose only 9%.
At this point, housing experts think young people need to get more creative in the home-buying process if they ever want a piece of the American dream.
"Well, one thing that's going on within the housing market is you're seeing — and this is also with the 21st Century housing bill that passed just several months ago — is you're going into blighted areas and investing in the rehabilitation of those homes. And that's actually a much cheaper way of owning a home than otherwise," Meredith Whitney, CEO of Meredith Whitney Advisory Group, said on Sozzi Unleashed.
"Detroit's the perfect example of this," she added, "where you had an economic revival with blighted areas, with run-down areas and investment in those areas. You can get a home for a massive discount to what you would have in the more established areas. And these areas are getting also economic investment from corporations. And you're seeing real revival."

item.title: GM beats on Q3 results, tightens profit outlook, unveils new $20 billion buyback
item.author: Pras Subramanian
item.description:
GM beats on Q3 results, tightens profit outlook, unveils new $20 billion buyback
2026-10-21
Por Pras Subramanian
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/gm-beats-on-q3-results-tightens-profit-outlook-unveils-new-20-billion-buyback-134307573.html
GM (GM) posted third quarter results before the bell that topped estimates, tightened its full-year profit outlook instead of boosting it, but issued shareholders a new $20 billion share repurchase program instead.
For the quarter, GM posted Q3 revenue of $50.0 billion, up 2.9% from a year ago and above the $48.52 billion Bloomberg consensus. GM posted adjusted EPS of $3.70 versus $3.57 estimated, with adjusted EBIT coming in at $4.1 billion, ahead of the $4.02 billion expected and up nearly 22%.
But the big update was guidance. For the full year, GM now expects:
- Adjusted EBIT of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion (prior $14 billion to $16 billion)
- Adjusted EPS of $12.75 to $13.75 (prior $12 to $14)
- Adjusted automotive free cash flow of $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion (prior $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion)
Investors were hoping for more, as the stock is getting hit in early trading, down over 5%.
Both ranges keep the same midpoints as before — $15 billion and $13.25 billion — meaning GM trimmed the upside as much as the downside.
GM also lifted its adjusted automotive free cash flow forecast to $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion from $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion.
GM's board approved a new $20 billion multiyear authorization with no expiration date. GM also declared a quarterly dividend of $0.18 per share.
"We think this is a proven strategy," GM CEO Mary Barra wrote in her letter to shareholders. "The new $20 billion multiyear share repurchase authorization we announced today further demonstrates our board's commitment to creating even greater shareholder value."
Barra also said GM is working to continue its momentum "despite growing inflationary pressures."
This is seen with GM's costs creeping up. GM now expects commodity inflation of about $2 billion (the top of its prior $1.5 billion-$2 billion range), including logistics and memory chip (DRAM) costs. It also cut its expected regulatory benefits to about $500 million from as much as $750 million. Offsetting that, gross tariff costs are tracking toward the low end of its $2.5 billion-$3.5 billion range.
Earlier this month, GM reported third quarter US sales of 670,974 vehicles, a drop of 5.5% compared to a year ago, as a collapse in EV sales offset gains from its pickups and small SUVs.
Based on GM's model-by-model figures, EV sales fell about 62% to roughly 25.5K units, shrinking to under 4% of GM's US volume from more than 9% a year ago. Excluding EVs, GM's sales were essentially flat, up 0.3%.
Sales of the Chevrolet Equinox EV plunged 92.4% to 1,905, the Blazer EV dropped 84.4%, the GMC Hummer EV slid 72.9%, and the Cadillac Lyriq fell 50.5%.

item.title: Anthropic May Spend $750 Billion on Computing Costs, Report Says
item.author: David Morris
item.description:
Anthropic May Spend $750 Billion on Computing Costs, Report Says
2026-10-21
Por David Morris
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/anthropic-may-spend-750-billion-200421561.html
(Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC could spend $750 billion on additional computing power in the coming years, according to a Wall Street Journal report, as the company prepares for an initial public offering.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The artificial intelligence firm had a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, the media outlet reported, citing a draft IPO prospectus. That compares to a net loss of $13 billion in the corresponding period a year ago, WSJ said.
The overwhelming majority of the net loss in the first half of this year, $72 billion, resulted from accounting charges linked to changes in the value of convertible notes and other instruments Anthropic has issued, according to the report.
Anthropic, one of the leading AI developers, is expected to publicly file paperwork for a Wall Street debut in the coming weeks, setting it up for what could be one of the largest IPOs ever. The listing will help the company raise additional capital to support its investments in chips, data centers and talent to build new and better AI models.
The company behind Claude spent close to $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the six months ended June 30, versus $2.3 billion in the same period in 2025, according to the Journal. Anthropic deployed more funds to secure computing power in the first half of 2026 than in all of 2025, when it spent $7.3 billion.
The prospectus shows Anthropic's extensive web of computing power agreements — totaling around $450 billion in the next seven to 10 years — the majority of which can't be canceled, according to the Journal. The company plans to spend $111 billion on contracts with Alphabet Inc.'s Google Cloud, $110 billion with Amazon.com Inc.'s Amazon Web Services and $31 billion with Microsoft Corp.
Anthropic's prospectus flags the risk of damages caused by AI, including the potential for models to show "self-preserving" qualities to avoid being turned off, and responses that resemble "blackmail" to keep humans from preventing them from operating, the report shows. Anthropic could also face the risk of political resistance to building data centers in the US, where most of its capacity is, according to the Journal.
The company told investors it had achieved profitability in the third quarter on an adjusted basis, Bloomberg News has reported. Anthropic is generating positive free cash flow, had gross margin of 85% and an over 11% positive adjusted operating margin as of the third quarter, people familiar with the matter have said.

item.title: Netflix stock sinks after announcing Q3 earnings, Q4 revenue forecast falls short of estimates
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Netflix stock sinks after announcing Q3 earnings, Q4 revenue forecast falls short of estimates
2026-10-21
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/netflix-stock-sinks-after-announcing-q3-earnings-q4-revenue-forecast-falls-short-of-estimates-204545261.html
Netflix (NFLX) stock fell 6% in premarket trading on Wednesday as the streaming giant's Q4 revenue outlook came in below Wall Street estimates, signaling slower growth.
The company posted revenue of $12.87 billion in its fiscal third quarter, in line with analyst estimates. Earnings per share came in at $0.87, topping estimates of $0.82.
Fourth-quarter outlook for the company's top line, though, came in at $13.44 billion, short of the consensus analyst estimate of $13.51 billion.
Netflix also cut its 2026 ad revenue guidance from $3 billion to $2.7 billion due to a slower-than-expected rollout of certain ad product capabilities.
Wall Street has been laser-focused on engagement, which management argued was healthy given the response to this year's price increases.
When it comes to the US, "our engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years," Greg Peters, co-CEO of Netflix, said during the earnings call.
"But we know that we can do better…It's our goal to go from very good to great," he added.
Wall Street analysts were looking for signs on whether slowing engagement would bleed into the revenue growth numbers.
"That is exactly what we are seeing with the 4Q growth outlook," Geetha Ranganathan, senior media analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, told Yahoo Finance after the results were released.
"This kind of speaks to a slowing growth algorithm, which kind of spells trouble for the company without a doubt," she added.
The results follow the streaming giant's job-cutting plan and a leadership shake-up announced last week amid slowing viewer engagement.
Last week, former Disney executive Peter Rice was named Netflix's next chief content officer. Rice replaces Bela Bajaria, who worked at the streamer for nearly a decade and served as CCO since 2023.
Also last week, Netflix said it would cut 6% of its workforce, or about 1,000 employees, marking the company's largest reduction of employees since 2022.
The move comes as the company seeks to reinvigorate viewership growth and strengthen its content amid growing competition and short-form viewing habits.
Audiences have increasingly moved away from traditional television sets toward mobile devices, noted Piper Sandler director and senior research analyst Tom Champion in a recent interview.
item.content:encoded:
Netflix stock sinks after announcing Q3 earnings, Q4 revenue forecast falls short of estimates

2026-10-21

Por Ines Ferré

https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/netflix-stock-sinks-after-announcing-q3-earnings-q4-revenue-forecast-falls-short-of-estimates-204545261.html

Netflix (NFLX) stock fell 6% in premarket trading on Wednesday as the streaming giant's Q4 revenue outlook came in below Wall Street estimates, signaling slower growth.

The company posted revenue of $12.87 billion in its fiscal third quarter, in line with analyst estimates. Earnings per share came in at $0.87, topping estimates of $0.82.

Fourth-quarter outlook for the company's top line, though, came in at $13.44 billion, short of the consensus analyst estimate of $13.51 billion.

Netflix also cut its 2026 ad revenue guidance from $3 billion to $2.7 billion due to a slower-than-expected rollout of certain ad product capabilities.

Wall Street has been laser-focused on engagement, which management argued was healthy given the response to this year's price increases.

When it comes to the US, "our engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years," Greg Peters, co-CEO of Netflix, said during the earnings call.

"But we know that we can do better…It's our goal to go from very good to great," he added.

Wall Street analysts were looking for signs on whether slowing engagement would bleed into the revenue growth numbers.

"That is exactly what we are seeing with the 4Q growth outlook," Geetha Ranganathan, senior media analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, told Yahoo Finance after the results were released.

"This kind of speaks to a slowing growth algorithm, which kind of spells trouble for the company without a doubt," she added.

The results follow the streaming giant's job-cutting plan and a leadership shake-up announced last week amid slowing viewer engagement.

Last week, former Disney executive Peter Rice was named Netflix's next chief content officer. Rice replaces Bela Bajaria, who worked at the streamer for nearly a decade and served as CCO since 2023.

Also last week, Netflix said it would cut 6% of its workforce, or about 1,000 employees, marking the company's largest reduction of employees since 2022.

The move comes as the company seeks to reinvigorate viewership growth and strengthen its content amid growing competition and short-form viewing habits.

Audiences have increasingly moved away from traditional television sets toward mobile devices, noted Piper Sandler director and senior research analyst Tom Champion in a recent interview.

item.title: Mejor entorno de confianza
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
Mejor entorno de confianza
2026-10-20
Por Texto propio
¿Mejor entorno de confianza?
Pablo Lucio Paredes
Columna publicada en diario El Universo, sábado 12 de Septiembre de 2026.
Visita de Marco Rubio
Conocemos la posición global de EEUU con tres ejes claves. Uno, controlar el mercado del petróleo y tierras raras. Dos, evitar la expansión china en particular en Latinoamérica. Tres, frenar la explosión del fentanilo, grave problema en la sociedad americana. ¿Dónde entramos nosotros? Quizás en los tres, pero con una compleja duda ¿qué damos a cambio? ¿cómo nos posicionamos en este juego? Ojalá no sea lo que sucede en Venezuela y Bolivia donde la relación parece ir con graves negociados e intereses particulares.
Tema: la confianza.
Estemos conscientes que el desarrollo se sustenta en varios factores, unos más estrictamente económicos o legales, otros institucionales. ¿Qué es esto último? Una definición de la RAE “Una costumbre, regla o pauta social muy arraigada”. Efectivamente son los mecanismos explícitos o implícitos alrededor de los cuales funciona una sociedad. Uno de ellos, clave, es la confianza que se expresa así: “expectativa sobre la conducta futura (positiva) de los demás y (pre)condición necesaria para la cooperación humana y la vida en sociedad”. Esto se aplica a diversos ámbitos y preguntémonos cómo estamos en el país…
(Des)confianza entre personas.
Muchos trabajos muestran que no confiamos, más allá del círculo familiar muy cercano. Más bien “actuamos con viveza criolla” (mal) antes que los demás se aprovechen de nosotros. Ejemplo sencillo, el tráfico: ¿confiamos en que los demás actuarán correctamente? ¿un peatón en un paso zebra, confía que los vehículos le dejarán pasar? Y más ampliamente ¿creemos que la mayor parte de gente actuará honestamente en la mayor parte de casos, o corrupción y viveza siguen campantes?
(Des)confianza institucional.
¿Creemos que las leyes se aplican de manera justa para todos? En particular: ¿creemos que la justicia cumple su rol y no favorece al que es capaz de sobornar a los jueces? Y más ampliamente: ¿estamos o no, viendo cómo se utilizan la justicia y la política para perseguir a los adversarios (que obviamente merecen ser sancionados si han delinquido) pero jamás a los propios? Opiniones negativas sobre el pasado y desgraciadamente igual ahora.
(Des)confianza económica.
Pregunta sencilla: si usted quiere ampliar su negocio invirtiendo o contratando más gente ¿su primera reacción es “hay los riesgos normales de cualquier negocio, pero me lanzo” o piensa dos veces y se frena porque “no confía en el entorno del país que es demasiado riesgoso”? Probablemente lo segundo. Claro, porque hay todo el tema de violencia desde las vacunas hasta los riesgos a la vida misma,
constantes limitaciones a la libertad y enorme irrespeto a los contratos. ¿En algo hemos mejorado? Sí en lo muy macro, así lo dice el excelente Índice de Incertidumbre de la USFQ: “aumentó en el segundo semestre 2025 e inicios 2026 por la eliminación del subsidio al
diésel, protestas y bloqueos, referéndum de noviembre, escalada de tensiones con Colombia, y desde febrero ha mejorado en un contexto de mayor estabilidad macroeconómica y retorno a los mercados internacionales” … Pero riesgos y desconfianza siguen ahí presentes frenando la calidad de vida, aumentando los costos de funcionamiento de la sociedad y (de)construyendo su estructura.

item.title: Amazon blocks agentic AI shopping. But Walmart is betting big that it's worth saying yes.
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
Amazon blocks agentic AI shopping. But Walmart is betting big that it's worth saying yes.
2026-10-20
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/amazon-blocks-agentic-ai-shopping-but-walmart-is-betting-big-that-its-worth-saying-yes-100000436.html
Americans like to shop. For a lot of consumers, the act of browsing and filling a digital or physical cart isn't a point of friction but a way of life — just ask Costco influencers.
But in the event that more people delegate their shopping to AI agents, Walmart, and its open embrace of AI partnerships, stands to win.
That's the takeaway in a new note by Bank of America analysts led by Christopher Nardone, published Monday. They cite Walmart's integration with multiple AI ecosystems; the development of the retailer's own shopping assistant named "Sparky"; and its partnerships with other agents, including Meta's Muse, as reasons for Walmart's solid positioning.
Walmart is among the key corporate players partnering with Muse, including Best Buy (BBY) and Ulta (ULTA). These companies are attempting to embrace new modes of digital commerce.
Other retailers have taken an antagonistic approach, choosing to block Muse from interacting with their commercial portals. No doubt there are a number of reasons to block largely untested agents from inserting themselves into your business funnel. But perhaps the most obvious is to prevent another tech platform from becoming a powerful middleman.
Amazon is perhaps the most notable example. The e-commerce giant has blocked Muse from making purchases on its site and prohibits other companies from deploying automated tools to shop.
But Amazon's loss could be Walmart's gain. While Amazon may not be losing much in the way of actual sales — since most people are using AI tools to research rather than to swipe the credit card, so to speak — Walmart is trying to get in early, while habits are still forming.
Still, Walmart's management team, like everyone else, can't say for certain how popular shopping agents will become. And there are other business implications to consider if agents disrupt how people shop. As Nardone noted, if screenless computers are the ones checking out, it remains unclear what happens to the advertising landscape, a business increasingly important to Walmart itself.
Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban.

item.title: US bank stocks' longest losing streak since 2008 clashes with earnings picture
item.author: David Hollerith
item.description:
US bank stocks' longest losing streak since 2008 clashes with earnings picture
2026-10-20
Por David Hollerith
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/us-bank-stocks-longest-losing-streak-since-2008-clashes-with-earnings-picture-165407807.html
US bank stocks are suffering their longest losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis, despite some of the country's biggest lenders having so far reported another sturdy set of earnings.
Results from the four biggest lenders last week gave fresh evidence that their US consumer and business customers are holding up even in the face of sharply elevated borrowing costs.
JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Bank of America (BAC), Citigroup (C), and Wells Fargo (WFC) collectively set aside $7.6 billion in credit provisions during the quarter, down about 3% from a year earlier. Actual loan losses in the quarter between these same banks fell 5%, while lending grew nearly 10%.
Investors still appear unconvinced. The benchmark KBW Nasdaq Bank Index (^BKX) fell slightly on Monday. It has sold off for the past six consecutive weeks, losing 11% since early September in its longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis, according to Yahoo Finance data.
Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility
The sell-off comes as credit managers worldwide appear increasingly worried about what happens next.
A recent survey of credit portfolio managers at major banks and other global financial institutions found that about 60% expect corporate defaults to rise worldwide over the next 12 months, while 85% anticipate wider spreads on North American junk bonds over the next three months. The figure is sharply higher compared to the survey's second quarter reading of a 40% rise in corporate defaults over the next 12 months and 50% increase in North American junk bonds in the ensuing three months.
Credit portfolio managers "are seeing some risk appetite among investors, but they are also seeing a number of companies, which have so far managed to stay afloat, beginning to reach the end of the line," Som-lok Leung, executive director for the International Association of Credit Portfolio Managers, said in an emailed statement.
Morgan Stanley analysts said in a Monday note to clients that bank credit conditions remain largely "benign," apart from isolated commercial weakness, although executives have sounded generally more cautious on earnings calls so far this month than in the second quarter.
Investor worries center on whether persistently higher interest rates will eventually squeeze borrowers. By the same logic, declining interest rates have "the potential to engineer a bounce" in bank stocks, Bank of America analyst Ebrahim Poonawala wrote Monday.
"Ideally, that occurs on the back of lower energy prices or easing inflation," Poonawala added.

Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility
The sell-off comes as credit managers worldwide appear increasingly worried about what happens next.
A recent survey of credit portfolio managers at major banks and other global financial institutions found that about 60% expect corporate defaults to rise worldwide over the next 12 months, while 85% anticipate wider spreads on North American junk bonds over the next three months. The figure is sharply higher compared to the survey's second quarter reading of a 40% rise in corporate defaults over the next 12 months and 50% increase in North American junk bonds in the ensuing three months.
Credit portfolio managers "are seeing some risk appetite among investors, but they are also seeing a number of companies, which have so far managed to stay afloat, beginning to reach the end of the line," Som-lok Leung, executive director for the International Association of Credit Portfolio Managers, said in an emailed statement.
Morgan Stanley analysts said in a Monday note to clients that bank credit conditions remain largely "benign," apart from isolated commercial weakness, although executives have sounded generally more cautious on earnings calls so far this month than in the second quarter.
Investor worries center on whether persistently higher interest rates will eventually squeeze borrowers. By the same logic, declining interest rates have "the potential to engineer a bounce" in bank stocks, Bank of America analyst Ebrahim Poonawala wrote Monday.
"Ideally, that occurs on the back of lower energy prices or easing inflation," Poonawala added.

item.title: Worried about a bigger tech stock rout? Find some comfort in this chart.
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Worried about a bigger tech stock rout? Find some comfort in this chart.
2026-10-20
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/worried-about-a-bigger-tech-stock-rout-find-some-comfort-in-this-chart-144823122.html
After a brutal stretch for momentum tech stocks the past week, some investors may be warming up to the view that it's time to cash in their chips and head for the hills.
While that is understandable, it's important to keep two things in mind on tech names.
First, major tech stock pullbacks are normal in a bull market, Truist chief markets strategist Keith Lerner pointed out.
Since this bull market began in October 2022, the S&P 500 tech sector has experienced 12 five-day declines of more than 6% and five double-digit pullbacks ranging from 10% to 26%, Lerner said. Semiconductors have experienced five 10-day declines exceeding 15%.
The second point is that the long-term trend on tech is still higher even considering these routs.
Despite these setbacks, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (^SOX) has gained more than 400% during this current bull market. The Technology sector (XLK) has gained 238%, more than double the S&P 500's (^GSPC) 114% return.
All of this is not to downplay what the market has recently digested on tech.
AI chip darling Nvidia (NVDA) shed more than $350 billion in market value last week. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than 11%.
Neocloud CoreWeave (CRWV) shed 25% on the week amid rising borrowing costs.
The returning concern: Revenue may not match the billions of dollars companies are investing in AI. How that unfolds for companies using massive amounts of debt to fund their AI investments is a top worry right now.
"The tech love-hate relationship continues. A once-in-a-generation technological advancement offers significant potential, but the wide range of outcomes and the difficulty identifying long-term winners and losers amplify each narrative and data point," Lerner said. "The recent weakness should be viewed in the context of these outsized gains."

item.title: 2 charts show why Wall Street is right to worry about tech stocks
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
2 charts show why Wall Street is right to worry about tech stocks
2026-10-20
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/2-charts-show-why-wall-street-is-right-to-worry-about-tech-stocks-145612923.html
The market is correct in the moment to voice concerns about how the rising cost of capital will impact hyperscalers' financial statements in 2027.
That is because hyperscalers such as Oracle (ORCL) and Google (GOOG, GOOGL) will need fresh debt to fuel their AI infrastructure builds, with free cash flow likely going negative.
JPMorgan strategist Mislav Matejka captured the situation perfectly in the two new charts below.
Hyperscaler free cash flow is forecast to turn negative in 2027, which implies that funding from credit markets is likely to drive more of the AI build-out going forward.
Current consensus estimates for hyperscaler capital expenditures in 2027 are already climbing from levels experts believe are now too low.
Morgan Stanley sees $1.6 trillion in total 2027 capital expenditures among the hyperscalers, up from $978 billion estimated for this year.
"The use cases are accelerating and we see it in the field every day and the capex dollars will be in the trillions with a massive ripple impact across the economy," Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives says. "We expect over 1,000 datacenters to be built over the next few years as this next phase of the AI Revolution is set to get built out."

item.title: The stock market isn’t the economy, but it’s influencing it like never before
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
The stock market isn’t the economy, but it’s influencing it like never before
2026-10-20
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/stocks-are-driving-consumption-like-never-before--and-that-exposes-a-big-risk-100000963.html
The stock market isn't the economy in the way that Nvidia's share price won't help your nephew find a job, or save for a down payment, or afford double meat and guac at Chipotle.
There's a level of abstraction and distance from day-to-day, working-class life that can make stock watching seem exotic. But the enormous gains of equity holdings in recent years have changed the makeup and definition of wealth in the US, with even bigger implications.
In a way that has only become true in our moment, the stock market actually is getting closer to defining the economy and consumption.
That's one of the key arguments in a note by Doug Peta, chief US investment strategist at BCA Research, published on Monday.
"The stock market isn't the economy, but it's influencing it like never before," he wrote. Peta observed that household net worth was over eight times disposable income at midyear, marking an all-time high for that measure. For decades, Wall Street has delivered outsized, compounding returns, making equities and mutual funds an ever-greater portion of household wealth.
The value of households' equity stake is nearly three times their annual after-tax income, Peta found. That means the S&P 500 gaining 10% in a year boosts a household's capacity to spend equivalent to receiving a 28% raise.
As a result, Peta wrote, stock market moves can swing consumption and overall economic activity. Combined with sharp home price appreciation, surging portfolios have augmented consumers' firepower far more than in any previous cycle, he said.
This helps explain the years-long narrative of the resilient American consumer. The people who spent their way through COVID, the aftermath, and sustained periods of high inflation. Stocks making up a higher share of a household's net worth has meant consumption is more sensitive to equity market moves. In good times, stock upswings can override other factors weighing down the economy.
"Greater sensitivity has been a boon for activity in the current cycle, as increasing equity wealth has allowed households to spend more of their paychecks than they otherwise may have," Peta wrote.
But that sensitivity is two-sided.
If the way the Wall Street winds are blowing has a greater say on the American consumer — because stock holdings increasingly define American wealth — that means the next bear market will have amplified influence.
Because instead of people feeling rich and spending through it, they will feel vulnerable and pull back.
In that very real sense, the stock market and the economy would sink together.
Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban.

item.title: Last week saw the largest tech sell skew in more than 5 years, Jefferies says
item.author: Jake Conley
item.description:
Last week saw the largest tech sell skew in more than 5 years, Jefferies says
2026-10-20
Por Jake Conley
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/last-week-saw-the-largest-tech-sell-skew-in-more-than-5-years-jefferies-says-173834306.html
Jefferies' equity trading desk saw its most heavily selling-tilted tech trading week in more than five years, analysts said over the weekend, putting a finer point on the CoreWeave-led tech sell-off that dominated markets last week.
"Simply put, there's a tremendous amount of angst in the market right now, and from our conversations and flows, there's been a very consistent and violent de-gross occurring over the last several sessions," Jeffrey Favuzza, TMT equity strategist at Jefferies, wrote to clients.
By market close on Friday, the week's skew in tech equities had reached $7.5 billion in net selling activity — a significant jump over the $5.5 billion skew ahead of the opening bell on Friday and a testament to heavy selling into the weekend.
The jump in outflow activity was enough to push the week's skew past that of the "DeepSeek moment" week in January 2025, when the Chinese AI lab released its open-weight DeepSeek model and set off a flurry of concerns that US labs would see their revenues fall as enterprises turned to cheaper foreign options, the analysts said.
Selling activity through Jefferies' equity trading desk was most concentrated last week in semiconductors, memory, hardware, and communications equipment subsectors, Favuzza noted, while only horizontal software and IT/info services subsectors saw a notable buy skew on the week.
That split matched activity in the wider market, where the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell by roughly 3% while the Philadelphia Semiconductor index (^SOX) lost 10%.
Much of the problem, Favuzza noted, lies with an increasingly sketchy financing picture. Part and parcel of the AI boom is the explosion in capex across the sector, with capex by hyperscalers alone expected to exceed $800 billion in 2026 and cross $1 trillion next year.
That spending has collided with a range of factors — the war in Iran, growing US debt, trade turmoil — that have pushed the international bond complex into a deep sell-off, sending yields on government debt from the US and other nations to multi-decade highs "at the same time that the hyperscalers have flooded the market with paper this year."
Last week's sell-off was largely catalyzed by spiking credit risk and worries about the worthiness of debt issuance at CoreWeave (CRWV), a so-called neocloud that's heavily backed by Nvidia (NVDA).
"While the underlying demand for the Neos hasn't downticked," Favuzza wrote to clients, "the confidence in some of their access to cheaper capital has."
The tech trade has also lost some of the momentum-driven wind in its sails, Favuzza said, arguing that "we never recovered, both from a price and conviction standpoint, from the Momentum meltdown of the summer." Not only was last week the worst in more than five years by sell skew, but it was also the second-worst week for the tech momentum pair (buying winning tech stocks while selling losers) in more than 20 years, beaten out only by a COVID-19 sell-off.

item.title: Goldman Sachs is still betting on a nice year-end rally for the S&P 500
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Goldman Sachs is still betting on a nice year-end rally for the S&P 500
2026-10-20
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/goldman-sachs-is-still-betting-on-a-nice-year-end-rally-for-the-sp-500-134755098.html
Momentum tech stocks tied to the AI boom may be triggering market tremors, but Goldman Sachs still thinks the year will end just fine for investors.
In a new note, Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider maintained his 8,000 year-end S&P 500 (^GSPC) price target. His target assumes about 5% upside from the current level of 7,659.
If Snider was concerned about an AI bubble bursting — as investors on X are chatting about seemingly around the clock — he isn't showing it in his 2027 S&P 500 target either. He sees the S&P 500 wrapping up next year at 8,700.
"Positive but decelerating growth has historically been associated with positive but moderating S&P 500 returns. Equity returns in these environments have historically been driven by earnings growth rather than by valuation expansion," Snider said.
Snider is modeling for 36% earnings growth for the S&P 500 this year, cooling to an 11% increase in 2027.
Snider's defense of a solidly bullish outlook comes as the very driver of markets this year — tech stocks playing a key role in the AI boom — fall under increased scrutiny by investors.
The returning concern: Revenue may not match the billions of dollars companies are investing in AI. How that unfolds for companies using massive amounts of debt to fund their AI investments is a top worry right now.
AI chip darling Nvidia (NVDA) shed more than $350 billion in market value last week. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOXX) plunged more than 11%.
Neocloud CoreWeave (CRWV) shed 25% on the week amid rising borrowing costs.
"This [move in CRWV] is more sentiment-driven. This is not about fundamentals," BofA analyst Tal Liani said on Sozzi Unleashed. "This is not about them not being able to pay for the debt, et cetera. This is more sentiment-driven, and the sentiment needs to change. And what's going to happen is, as always, there's going to be a period of concern. And then the fundamentals will kick in, meaning revenues, revenue growth."

item.title: Elon Musk says he's giving SpaceX stock to every kid in America
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Elon Musk says he's giving SpaceX stock to every kid in America
2026-10-20
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/elon-musk-says-hes-giving-spacex-stock-to-every-kid-in-america-131435467.html
Kids will soon have a financial interest in the future of space.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX (SPCX) shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said in an X post on Monday.
Musk didn't specify an age range for the proposed gift, but a Bloomberg report indicated he could use Trump Accounts as the vehicle for his stock donations.
SpaceX stock rose 1% in morning trading on Monday.
There are currently about 73 million children under 18 living in the US, according to the latest Census Bureau data. That number goes down to about 18.5 million for newborns up to 4 years old.
SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell has already pledged a personal donation of more than $320 million in SpaceX stock to fund Trump Accounts for more than 2 million children.

item.title: Palantir, Datadog and chip stocks bounce back as Amazon lifts Wall Street
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Palantir, Datadog and chip stocks bounce back as Amazon lifts Wall Street
2026-10-20
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/palantir-datadog-and-chip-stocks-bounce-back-as-amazon-lifts-wall-street-204043191.html
Tech stocks got off the mat Monday. Most of Wall Street stayed pinned down.
Palantir (PLTR) and Datadog (DDOG) jumped over 4% each, joined by Snowflake (SNOW) and a broad recovery in chip stocks after last week's beating.
Western Digital (WDC) and Sandisk (SNDK) led the storage rally, while Micron (MU), Intel (INTC), and Nvidia (NVDA) also gained. More than 9 in 10 semiconductor names and roughly 4 in 5 software stocks advanced in Yahoo Finance's watchlists.
Buyers had fresh encouragement. Bernstein upgraded Datadog, citing stronger AI-related demand. Palantir announced a government-cloud partnership, although its rebound reached a potential selling zone around $195–$200. Getting through that area would put its recent record high back in play and lend support to the broader recovery after last week's failed breakouts.
Amazon (AMZN) supplied some heavyweight help. Shares climbed 5%, recovering last week's losses after Morgan Stanley named the company a top pick. Tesla (TSLA) also rallied.
Together, those gains helped the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) rise 1.1%, and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) add 0.4%.
But buyers weren't handing out second chances to everyone.
"We can't just go and buy all the AI companies because they all dipped," Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, told Yahoo Finance.
CoreWeave (CRWV) provided a case in point. Its early rally after a Goldman Sachs upgrade to Buy disappeared. Shares finished slightly lower at $61.12, just above July's closing low of $60.82.
The trouble wasn't limited to CoreWeave. Nearly two-thirds of S&P 500 stocks fell, and the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) lost ground. The broader index rose, but most of its stocks fell.
Tuesday's test is whether more stocks join the rebound and CoreWeave can pull away from its July low.

item.title: John Ternus Is Engineering a New Era for Apple: The Best Inventions of 2026
item.author: Andrew R Chow; Cupertino; Calif
item.description:
John Ternus Is Engineering a New Era for Apple: The Best Inventions of 2026
2026-10-20
Por Andrew R Chow; Cupertino; Calif
https://time.com/collection/best-inventions/2026/apple-iphone-duo/
Just below the broad smile he’s been wearing all morning, John Ternus’ hands are shaking.
On this September day in Silicon Valley, Apple’s new CEO is surrounded by celebrities, tech enthusiasts, and reporters who have flocked to Apple Park from around the world to catch a glimpse of the company’s new and long-awaited foldable phone, the Duo. After Ternus takes a few photos with the device, an Apple PR rep pulls the influencer known as IShowSpeed out of the crowd to meet him. Winning over the 21-year-old isn’t exactly the toughest assignment Ternus has faced in his 25-year Apple career: Speed barks when he sees the phone and then gleefully springs into a backflip.
Ternus, who took over as CEO on Sept. 1, was chosen to run Apple because he has ably applied his engineering and design expertise to shape products that redefined entire categories of technology, from the Mac to iPad to AirPods and the iPhone. But becoming the face and front man for the second biggest company in the world by market cap is another proposition entirely. Ternus’ hard technical skills may not translate easily to a position that involves toggling from Hollywood to stockholders, to politicians shaping policy, to rival CEOs in the constellation of tech companies whose power challenges nation-states.
His predecessor, Tim Cook, gained stature on the world stage as a power broker deftly navigating global politics, markets, and supply chains. Cook’s predecessor, Steve Jobs, was a rock-star visionary who sold the world on the deeply personal and even spiritual nature of tech creations. Ternus is different from both: a private, detail-oriented engineer, little known outside the company until he became a senior hardware executive in 2021.
Rather than try to replicate his forerunners’ styles of success, Ternus has so far played to his own strengths—which are also those of Apple, a company that first and foremost builds beautiful products that spark productivity, creativity, and joy. Ternus’ interaction with IShowSpeed is clearly designed to capture this (and, of course, to goose preorder numbers among the influencer’s young and massive audience). To some critics, however, the scene might read as a legacy company aura-farming to sell expensive gizmos instead of building the actual technological future, which is artificial intelligence.
Virtually every one of Apple’s fellow Goliaths—Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, and now Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic—have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years. At the end of September, Apple was conspicuously absent when President Donald Trump hosted a luncheon for AI power players like SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Google’s Sundar Pichai, who lobbied him on their visions for America’s tech future.
But Ternus and other Apple executives say they aren’t concerned. In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley’s “lunatic fringe,” as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it. And besides, Ternus argues, even if other companies succeed in their mission of building super-intelligence, users will still want to talk to it on Apple devices.
“People want physical things,” he says a week later at the company’s flagship store on Fifth Avenue in New York City, wearing an amiable but guarded smile. He spent the morning greeting superfans who
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Netflix faces questions on user engagement ahead of third-quarter report
item.author: Reuters
item.description:
Netflix faces questions on user engagement ahead of third-quarter report
2026-10-20
Por Reuters
https://finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/articles/netflix-faces-questions-user-engagement-101735340.html
Oct 19 (Reuters) - Netflix investors are expecting details on how the streaming giant plans to sustain growth when it reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, as competition intensifies and user engagement shows signs of fatigue.
Ted Sarandos, the co-CEO of Netflix, recently admitted the company "is not growing as fast as I want us to", and suggested live programming could be an opportunity to accelerate growth.
Here are more details:
• Netflix is expected to post its slowest third-quarter revenue growth in three years, with sales forecast to increase 11.8% to $12.87 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
• It cut about 6% of its workforce in a move that analyst Ross Benes of Emarketer said reflected the streaming industry's shift to profitability.
• Netflix also saw a change in its content leadership, with longtime head of content Bela Bajaria leaving the company and former Disney executive Peter Rice taking over.
• Its US user churn rose 16.6% year-over-year in the third quarter, roughly double the pace of the prior three quarters, while downloads in the US and Canada fell 20%, according to market research firm Apptopia.
• Jefferies estimates average monthly viewing time per Netflix member fell to 49 hours in the first half of this year from 66 hours in the first half of 2023.
• The 2026 FIFA World Cup and a weaker content slate than last year weighed on Netflix's engagement, analysts said.
• The company recently acquired broadcast rights to air the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra.
• Netflix is betting on advertising to diversify revenue, with Jefferies forecasting ad revenue to reach $7.5 billion in 2029.

item.content:encoded:
Netflix faces questions on user engagement ahead of third-quarter report

2026-10-20

Por Reuters

https://finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/articles/netflix-faces-questions-user-engagement-101735340.html

Oct 19 (Reuters) - Netflix investors are expecting details on how the streaming giant plans to sustain growth when it reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, as competition intensifies and user engagement shows signs of fatigue.

Ted Sarandos, the co-CEO of Netflix, recently admitted the company "is not growing as fast as I want us to", and suggested live programming could be an opportunity to accelerate growth.

Here are more details:

• Netflix is expected to post its slowest third-quarter revenue growth in three years, with sales forecast to increase 11.8% to $12.87 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

• It cut about 6% of its workforce in a move that analyst Ross Benes of Emarketer said reflected the streaming industry's shift to profitability.

• Netflix also saw a change in its content leadership, with longtime head of content Bela Bajaria leaving the company and former Disney executive Peter Rice taking over.

• Its US user churn rose 16.6% year-over-year in the third quarter, roughly double the pace of the prior three quarters, while downloads in the US and Canada fell 20%, according to market research firm Apptopia.

• Jefferies estimates average monthly viewing time per Netflix member fell to 49 hours in the first half of this year from 66 hours in the first half of 2023.

• The 2026 FIFA World Cup and a weaker content slate than last year weighed on Netflix's engagement, analysts said.

• The company recently acquired broadcast rights to air the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra.

• Netflix is betting on advertising to diversify revenue, with Jefferies forecasting ad revenue to reach $7.5 billion in 2029.

(Reporting by Harshita Mary Varghese in Bengaluru; Editing by Edmund Lee and Devika Syamnath)

item.title: Why Is Tech Billionaire Marc Andreessen So Mad
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
Why Is Tech Billionaire Marc Andreessen So Mad
2026-10-19
Por Texto propio
# Why Is Tech Billionaire Marc Andreessen So Mad?
October 15, 2026
The prominent investor has said the Biden administration pushed him to the political right, but sources say his grievances don't always match reality.
By Austin Carr
Marc Andreessen sounded angry. It was May 22, 2024, and he was venting to a table full of President Joe Biden's officials in the West Wing office of Jeff Zients, then the White House chief of staff. The famed venture capitalist was in town with his longtime investing partner, Ben Horowitz, to discuss US tech policy, and the private lunch soon turned heated. Andreessen expressed his frustration about a slew of Biden administration initiatives and regulations, especially ones he believed were crippling the artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency industries. Near the end of the lunch, he also launched into a tirade against a Democratic proposal to hike taxes on the wealthiest 0.01% of American households. "The billionaire tax seemed to offend him more than anything we'd done on AI or even crypto," says Bruce Reed, one of the handful of White House advisers who had joined the meeting.
Forgotten, at least, until Donald Trump won the election months later and Andreessen revealed in the aftermath the crazy reason why he had unexpectedly plowed millions of dollars into the Make America Great Again movement during the campaign. Andreessen, who voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016 and said back then that Trump's immigration regime "makes me sick to my stomach," explained on a podcast that he was compelled by "absolutely horrifying" discussions he once had with Biden officials. In his retelling, they divulged a top-secret plan for the federal government to take control of the AI industry and outlaw all startups and open-source software. "You guys think you can just start companies and write code and release code on the internet—those days are over," he remembered them warning in the meeting.
Andreessen was so aghast that he felt it was in the best interest of his firm, Andreessen Horowitz, which is known as a16z, to publicly endorse Trump. "They're going to kill us," Andreessen recalled thinking on Ross Douthat's podcast in January 2025. "We walked out and stood in the parking lot of the West Wing and took one look at each other, and we're like, 'Yeah, we're for Trump.'" (Horowitz later hedged his support when Kamala Harris replaced Biden in the race, and he made a significant personal donation.)
The incident became Silicon Valley lore, but at first the Biden-Harris camp couldn't even figure out what meeting Andreessen was referring to, according to four people familiar with the situation. When they finally realized he was talking about the lunch in Zients' office, those who attended were baffled: Andreessen is prone to hyperbole, but this neared complete fiction. "It is simply false that the Biden administration told Andreessen and Horowitz that the government would ban all AI startups," says Ben Buchanan, then a special adviser to the president on AI, who attended the May 22 meeting. It also made little sense why Andreessen hadn't asked about this astonishingly draconian plan at a meeting on May 24 with national security advisers including Anne Neuberger. (Neuberger, whom a16z has since hired, declined to comment.) As another top Biden official familiar with their visits told colleagues of Andreessen's version of events: "Total bulls---."
A representative for Andreessen, Horowitz and a16z's government affairs chief, Collin McCune, who also attended the contentious meeting in DC, has said the firm stands by their recollections. (Horowitz and McCune didn't respond to requests for comment for this article.) Whatever actually occurred at that lunch matters less than what's happened since: a16z, known for Andreessen once proclaiming that "software is eating the world," is now eating the political world. The dominant VC firm, wh
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Peter Schiff warns a ‘perfect storm of financial destruction’ worse than 2008 is brewing. Build wealth beyond your home
item.author: Thomas Kent
item.description:
Peter Schiff warns a ‘perfect storm of financial destruction’ worse than 2008 is brewing. Build wealth beyond your home
2026-10-19
Por Thomas Kent
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/peter-schiff-warns-perfect-storm-110500854.html
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.
The low mortgage rate you locked in years ago might be one of your best financial decisions. Peter Schiff argued it could also be part of a "perfect storm of financial destruction that is about to hit."
"Mortgage lenders will lose far more during the developing mortgage crisis than they did during all of the GFC," Schiff warned in an Oct. 15 post on X (1), referring to the global financial crisis.
A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Priority Gold's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free
He claimed, "Even without a single default, on paper mortgage lenders have already lost over four times more than they lost during the GFC."
He blamed the Federal Reserve's prolonged low interest rates and government-backed mortgages that let borrowers lock in cheap financing for decades.
"That sowed the seeds," he wrote.
An alarming forecast, especially if your home represents much of your wealth or you're counting on your investments to carry you through retirement.
But before you start picturing another foreclosure crisis, there's an important distinction: A mortgage losing value to an investor doesn't automatically mean your house has lost value, your payment is going up, or your lender is about to fail.
And keep in mind, if your loan or its servicing changes hands, the new company can't just rewrite your agreement (2).
Why Schiff sees trouble in low-rate mortgages
"There is currently about $8.3 trillion in outstanding fixed-rate mortgages with an average rate of 4.6% and 25 years left to maturity," Schiff wrote. "Given that current rates are 7.5%, the mark-to-market losses on those mortgages are already about $2 trillion. When rates rise to 8.5%, the loss will rise to $3 trillion!"
For comparison, Schiff put realized losses on defaulted mortgages during 2007–2010 at about $450 billion.
Keep in mind these are Schiff's estimates, and his 8.5% scenario isn't today's reality. The latest Freddie Mac survey (3), released Oct. 15, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.40%, up from 6.27% a year earlier.
Here's the basic pricing problem: If a new mortgage pays a substantially higher rate, an investor generally won't pay full price for an otherwise comparable older loan paying much less. The older loan then needs a discount to compete.
That decline in market value is the paper loss Schiff is describing. The homeowner could still be making every payment on time.
Schiff puts two different types of losses side by side — money lost when borrowers default, and declines in what performing loans could fetch in a sale.
A mortgage can lose resale value even while homeowners keep making payments. That can hurt whoever owns the loan, but it isn't the same as a borrower defaulting.
Who owns the loan matters. Mortgages are often sold and packaged into securities (4) whose investors receive payments from pools of borrowers. So, the company that originated your mortgage isn't necessarily the one carrying its investment risk going forward.
You don't have to accept Schiff's prediction to examine your own exposure. If your home accounts for much of your wealth, how much have you built outside it?
Consider gold alongside your other assets
If much of your wealth is tied up in property, building investments outside housing can give you exposure to different sources of returns.
A gold IRA is one option for adding physical precious metals to your retirement portfolio. Gold is often used as a potential hedge against inflation and economic uncert
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Official data show China is dumping more U.S. Treasury debt. But it may actually be a stealth buyer, with a big stash suspiciously piling up in Canada
item.author: Jason Ma
item.description:
Official data show China is dumping more U.S. Treasury debt. But it may actually be a stealth buyer, with a big stash suspiciously piling up in Canada
2026-10-19
Por Jason Ma
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/official-data-show-china-dumping-175844985.html
China was once the top holder of U.S. Treasuries but has been shedding its massive stockpile for years, fueling fears of de-dollarization, but official data may not fully capture Beijing's actual portfolio.
The decline began in earnest around 2021, but as recently as April 2022, China still held $1 trillion in Treasury securities. U.S. data on Friday show that's been whittled down to just $591 billion as of August, the lowest in 18 years and down from $700 billion a year earlier.
But the data is collected primarily from U.S.-based custodians and broker-dealers, according to the Treasury Department, which adds that U.S. securities held in overseas custody accounts may not be attributed to the actual owners.
As a result, China watchers have long been skeptical of a wholesale dumping of U.S. assets, pointing to suspicious jumps in Treasury holdings elsewhere that coincide with the steep Chinese drop.
Canada's holdings soared to $465 billion in August from just $169 billion in the same month five years ago. Similarly, Belgium's stockpile shot up to $490.5 billion from $228 billion over the same span. After including other bonds backed by federal housing agencies, the numbers are even more staggering.
To be sure, China has been challenging the U.S. for supremacy in global finance, seeking to unseat the dollar as the world's top currency.
U.S. sanctions against Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine further encouraged the People's Bank of China and other central banks around the world to diversify away from dollar reserves and toward alternative assets like gold.
President Donald Trump's trade war, which has been particularly focused on China, gave Beijing more reasons to ditch Treasuries and decouple from the U.S.
But at the same time, China has relied more heavily on export-led growth in recent years as domestic demand remains stagnant amid the festering property crash and debt hangover.
So despite the friction with the U.S. and other trade partners, China posted a $1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025—the largest in recorded history—growing three times faster than global goods trade.
This year looks to break that record. For the first nine months of 2026, China's trade surplus reached $938 billion, with expectations growing that it could surpass last year's milestone.
Such massive surpluses must be recycled back somewhere, perhaps leading China to shift its Treasury debt to non-U.S. custodian banks in other countries—and not show up as "China" in official U.S. data.
"The evidence that China uses a Canadian custodian for some of its Agencies is especially strong — note the sudden jump in Canada's holdings and the big impact of the detailed June survey at some early points," Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Treasury official, posted on X on Wednesday while highlighting a Bloomberg story on the subject.
